title: Demystifying English Tenses: A Step-by-Step Timeline Guide
dek: Understand English tenses step by step: time, tense and aspect, a timeline for each of the 12 forms, and which forms you really need in speech and writing.

blocks.title: Editorial Letter from Founder JY DM — November Academia
blocks.content: Dear readers, JY DM is here and I'd like to congratulate you on a new beginning of a new month, November, and our new issue "November Academia". I'm not sure about you, but for me November is quite an interesting time. Whilst many consider September to be the start of an educational process, for me it's about November. Whilst the beautiful season of autumn is wrapping up and a new magical season of winter begins, November is the perfect transition zone between them. In November, darkness becomes longer and I immediately imagine these dark evenings spent in the library while reading books, writing things. The air is already crisp, so we wear trenches, walk with books in our hands, wearing gloves and scarves — in a nutshell, the academia style. That's why our issue is about this.

blocks.text: Before you start: a simpler way to see English tenses
blocks.say: Before you start: a simpler way to see English tenses

blocks.text: Most learners meet tenses as one big table of 12 forms. The table is useful, but it hides a simple idea. A verb tells you three things at once: *when* something happens, *which form* the verb takes, and *how the speaker sees the action*. This guide adds one idea at a time, with a timeline for each form.

blocks.text: Step 1 (A2): Time, tense and aspect
blocks.say: Step 1 (A2): Time, tense and aspect

blocks.text: **Time** is reality: before now, now, or after now. **Tense** is the form of the verb. English verbs have a past form (*walked*) and a present form (*walk*), and we talk about the future with helpers such as *will* or *going to*. **Aspect** is how the speaker sees the action: *simple* (a fact or a whole event), *progressive* (in progress) or *perfect* (linked to another point in time).
blocks.say: Time is reality: before now, now, or after now. Tense is the form of the verb. English verbs have a past form (walked) and a present form (walk), and we talk about the future with helpers such as will or going to. Aspect is how the speaker sees the action: simple (a fact or a whole event), progressive (in progress) or perfect (linked to another point in time).

blocks.text: The "12 tenses" in coursebooks are 3 times multiplied by 4 aspects: simple, progressive, perfect and perfect progressive. It is a convenient teaching label, not the only description of English. Some grammars, such as Huddleston and Pullum's, say English has two tenses and express the future in other ways. Both views help; use the one that makes your learning easier.
blocks.say: The "12 tenses" in coursebooks are 3 times multiplied by 4 aspects: simple, progressive, perfect and perfect progressive. It is a convenient teaching label, not the only description of English. Some grammars, such as Huddleston and Pullum's, say English has two tenses and express the future in other ways. Both views help; use the one that makes your learning easier.

blocks.caption: The 12 forms: 3 times and 4 aspects
blocks.say: Here are the twelve forms with the verb work. Simple: I worked, I work, I will work. Progressive: I was working, I am working, I will be working. Perfect: I had worked, I have worked, I will have worked. Perfect progressive: I had been working, I have been working, I will have been working.

blocks.text: Step 2 (A2): Time markers are hints
blocks.say: Step 2 (A2): Time markers are hints

blocks.text: Words such as *yesterday* or *tomorrow* help you choose a form. Notice the difference between *in 2010* (a finished time) and *since 2010* (a time that continues until now).
blocks.say: Words such as yesterday or tomorrow help you choose a form. Notice the difference between in 2010 (a finished time) and since 2010 (a time that continues until now).

rows: yesterday, two days ago, last week, in 2010
Have you ever been to Brazil?
I am studying at the moment.
blocks.caption: Time markers and the forms they often go with
blocks.say: Yesterday, ago and in 2010 usually go with the past simple. Since and for go with the present perfect. Already, yet, just, ever and never also go with the present perfect. Right now and at the moment go with the present progressive. Tomorrow and next week go with future forms.

blocks.text: Markers are hints, not rules. *I'm leaving tomorrow* uses a present form for a future plan, and *I have lived here since 2020* uses a time marker with the present perfect.
blocks.say: Markers are hints, not rules. I'm leaving tomorrow uses a present form for a future plan, and I have lived here since 2020 uses a time marker with the present perfect.

blocks.text: Step 3 (A2): The simple forms
blocks.say: Step 3 (A2): The simple forms

blocks.text: The simple forms are the backbone of everyday English. They give facts, habits, routines and single events.
blocks.say: The simple forms are the backbone of everyday English. They give facts, habits, routines and single events.

blocks.gloss: Routine or general fact. Form: subject + base verb (he / she / it + -s)
blocks.say: Present simple: I drink coffee every morning.. Routine or general fact. Form: subject + base verb (he / she / it + -s).

blocks.text: Step 4 (A2 to B1): The progressive forms
blocks.say: Step 4 (A2 to B1): The progressive forms

blocks.text: Progressive forms show an action *in progress*. Think of a bar on the timeline, not a dot.
blocks.say: Progressive forms show an action in progress. Think of a bar on the timeline, not a dot.

blocks.gloss: In progress now. Form: am / is / are + verb-ing

blocks.text: **Careful:** verbs of state, such as *know, like, want* and *understand*, are rarely used in the progressive. Say *I know the answer*, not *I am knowing the answer*. In informal speech there are exceptions, so do not treat this as an absolute rule.

blocks.text: Step 5 (B1): The perfect forms
blocks.say: Step 5 (B1): The perfect forms

blocks.text: Perfect forms always link **two points in time**. The present perfect links the past to now. The past perfect links an earlier past event to a later past event. The future perfect looks back from a future deadline.
blocks.say: Perfect forms always link two points in time. The present perfect links the past to now. The past perfect links an earlier past event to a later past event. The future perfect looks back from a future deadline.

blocks.targetText: Present perfect: I have finished my assignment.
blocks.gloss: A past action with a link to now. Form: have / has + past participle
blocks.context: Level: B1. Result or experience matters now

blocks.text: Past simple or present perfect?
blocks.say: Past simple or present perfect?

rows: I lived in London for two years.
The period is finished. I no longer live there.
I have lived in London for two years.
The period continues until now. I still live there.
blocks.caption: A minimal pair: past simple and present perfect
blocks.say: Compare two sentences. I lived in London for two years means the period is finished and I no longer live there. I have lived in London for two years means the period continues until now and I still live there.

blocks.text: Use the past simple when the time is finished (*yesterday, in 2010, last year*). Use the present perfect when the time is not mentioned or is still open (*today, this week, since 2010, ever*).
blocks.say: Use the past simple when the time is finished (yesterday, in 2010, last year). Use the present perfect when the time is not mentioned or is still open (today, this week, since 2010, ever).

blocks.text: Step 6 (B2): The perfect progressive forms
blocks.say: Step 6 (B2): The perfect progressive forms

blocks.text: These forms answer the question: *how long has something been going on until a certain point?*

blocks.text: Tenses without time markers
blocks.say: Tenses without time markers

blocks.text: Native speakers rarely add *already*, *now* or *yesterday* to every sentence. The form of the verb carries the meaning.
blocks.say: Native speakers rarely add already, now or yesterday to every sentence. The form of the verb carries the meaning.

rows: Present perfect: *I've lost my library card.*
I have a problem now. I can't borrow books today.
Past simple: *I lost my library card.*
A finished event. The card may be found or replaced already.
Past progressive: *The snow was falling over the library.*
A background scene in a story.
Present progressive: *I'm meeting Anna at six.*
A fixed arrangement for the future, without saying *tomorrow*.
Past perfect: *The archivist had locked the doors.*
This happened first, before the main event in the story.
blocks.caption: What the form tells the listener
blocks.say: The form of the verb carries meaning. I've lost my library card means I have a problem now. I lost my library card is a finished event. The snow was falling is a background scene. I'm meeting Anna at six is a fixed arrangement. The archivist had locked the doors happened before the main event.

blocks.text: What do you really need in speech and in writing?
blocks.say: What do you really need in speech and in writing?

blocks.text: Everyday speech relies mostly on a small set of forms: present simple, past simple, present progressive, present perfect, and *will* or *going to* for the future. Very long forms, such as the future perfect progressive, are rare in conversation. This is a general pattern, not a figure from a specific study, so use it to set your priorities and not as a rule.
blocks.say: Everyday speech relies mostly on a small set of forms: present simple, past simple, present progressive, present perfect, and will or going to for the future. Very long forms, such as the future perfect progressive, are rare in conversation. This is a general pattern, not a figure from a specific study, so use it to set your priorities and not as a rule.

rows: I have worked here for years.
I am going to work. / I will work.
He had left before I came.
Present perfect progressive is common (*I have been working*). The others are rare.
Present perfect progressive is used for ongoing work; the others are rare.
blocks.caption: Where each form is most useful
blocks.say: The present simple, past simple, present perfect, present progressive and future forms are useful in both speech and writing. The past perfect appears in stories and in academic writing. The present perfect progressive is common in speech. The other perfect progressive forms are rare.

blocks.text: Quiz: choose the best form
blocks.say: Quiz: choose the best form

blocks.question: I ___ in Lyon for two years, and I still live here.
blocks.explanation: The situation continues until now, so use the present perfect: *I have lived*.
blocks.say: I in Lyon for two years, and I still live here. Think about it, then check the answer on the page.

blocks.question: She ___ me an hour ago.
blocks.explanation: *An hour ago* gives a finished time, so use the past simple.
blocks.say: She me an hour ago. Think about it, then check the answer on the page.

blocks.question: When I arrived, the film ___ already started.
blocks.explanation: The film started before I arrived, so use the past perfect: *had started*.
blocks.say: When I arrived, the film already started. Think about it, then check the answer on the page.

blocks.question: I ___ here since nine o'clock.
blocks.explanation: *Since nine o'clock* shows duration up to now, so use the present perfect progressive.
blocks.say: I here since nine o'clock. Think about it, then check the answer on the page.

blocks.question: By 5 PM, I ___ the report.
blocks.explanation: *By 5 PM* is a future deadline, so use the future perfect: *will have completed*.
blocks.say: By 5 PM, I the report. Think about it, then check the answer on the page.

blocks.question: I ___ the answer.
blocks.explanation: *Know* is a verb of state. It is normally used in the simple form.
blocks.say: I the answer. Think about it, then check the answer on the page.

blocks.question: Which sentence means the speaker lives in London now?
options: I lived in London for two years.
I have lived in London for two years.
I had lived in London for two years.
I would live in London for two years.
blocks.explanation: The present perfect links the past to now. The past simple and past perfect are about finished periods.

blocks.text: Summary: a plan for learners
blocks.say: Summary: a plan for learners

items: Separate **time**, **tense** and **aspect**. This makes the 12 forms easier to understand.
Use time markers as **hints**, not as rules.
Start with the simple forms and the present perfect. Compare past simple with present perfect often.
Add the progressive forms, then the perfect forms, and leave the long perfect progressive forms for last.
Learn the forms in whole sentences and notice what each one tells the listener.
blocks.say: Separate time, tense and aspect. This makes the 12 forms easier to understand. Use time markers as hints, not as rules. Start with the simple forms and the present perfect. Compare past simple with present perfect often. Add the progressive forms, then the perfect forms, and leave the long perfect progressive forms for last. Learn the forms in whole sentences and notice what each one tells the listener.
